articles.title: Brickbat: Mein Gott
articles.content: 德国最大警方工会副主席、联邦警察高级官员斯文·许伯（Sven Hüber）因媒体报道其过去的滥用指控和不当行为而辞职。据与其在1980年代后期共事的同事作证称，许伯在担任东德边境部队军官期间，曾对一名试图越境的男子施以虐待，将手枪塞入其口中并踢其面部。证词还指控许伯命令士兵对越境者实施“射杀”命令，并因一名哨所指挥官未执行命令而公开贬低并降职其。许伯否认了所有指控，称其为“虚假且有害”，并表示辞职是为了不影响工会的法律斗争。
articles.summary:
Sven Hüber, the deputy chairman of Germany's largest police union and a high-ranking government official with the Federal Police, has resigned after media reports brought up accusations of abuse and misconduct. While serving as an officer in the East German border troops in the late 1980s, Hüber allegedly mistreated a man trying to escape by pushing a pistol into his mouth and kicking him in the face, according to a sworn statement from someone who worked with him at the time. It further claims that he told soldiers to follow a shoot-to-kill order against people crossing the border, and when a post leader failed to shoot escapees, Hüber called him a traitor and publicly demoted him. Hüber denied the accusations as false and damaging, saying he stepped down so the legal fight does not hurt the union.

The post Brickbat: Mein Gott appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Why Conservative Republicans Are Worried About License Plate Cameras
articles.content:
Last month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott froze state funding for automated license plate readers (ALPRs), acknowledging concerns about the warrantless surveillance enabled by such AI-assisted cameras. Abbott took that step the day after Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a fellow Republican, declared that ALPRs are "out of control."
Both governors cited recent reports about police officers accused of using ALPR data for personal purposes, which seem to be driving a shift in public opinion about the technology. Such incidents highlight the perils of giving cops across the country easy access to such data, which they can use to track your travels, identify nearby vehicles, and even predict your itinerary, without judicial oversight or meaningful internal supervision.
Abbott mentioned a Lufkin, Texas, police officer who was charged with using ALPR information to stalk an ex-girlfriend, her relatives, and her acquaintances more than 10,000 times. DeSantis alluded to similar cases in Florida, where officers in Sarasota and Haines City had recently been arrested for misusing ALPR data.
"When I see, like, a police officer using this to track, like, an ex-girlfriend," DeSantis said, "I'm like, you know, what the hell's going on?" Local officials are beginning to ask the same question.
As of Tuesday, the Institute for Justice counted 181 local governments that have canceled or declined to renew ALPR contracts since the beginning of 2025. In Texas alone, The Dallas Express reports, at least 23 jurisdictions have dropped contracts, suspended service, or reduced the size of their ALPR networks.
Some 7,000 police departments have installed those networks, which include around 140,000 cameras, without giving much thought to the privacy implications or the potential for abuse. But some of them are now having second thoughts, reflecting rising public skepticism of unconstrained ALPR use.
In a YouGov survey last month, 46 percent of respondents opposed police use of ALPRs, including 31 percent who were "strongly" opposed, while 38 percent favored the practice. A year ago, by contrast, YouGov found that 45 percent of Americans supported ALPRs, while 33 percent opposed them, including 20 percent who were "strongly" opposed.
That reversal coincides with proliferating reports of blatant ALPR abuses. The Institute for Justice has identified "well over 100" such incidents, which it notes "may be just the tip of the iceberg" given the reality of lax oversight and widespread data sharing.
Police officers are supposed to use that information, which they can access on computers or mobile phones, only for legitimate law enforcement purposes. But as a Wichita police supervisor conceded in 2024, it's "not even possible" to enforce that policy by making sure that each search complies with it.
Compounding that challenge, each agency typically shares ALPR information with many others. Once that happens, The Wichita Eagle noted in 2022, local police officials have "no control over how those outside agencies use it and no way to flag unlawful searches."
In Norfolk, Virginia, a local radio station reported last April, police officers often give "incomplete and imprecise reasons" for ALPR searches, including "suspect," "suspicious," and "investigation" or "inv." Such vague labels hardly seem consistent with a state law requiring that cops state a "specific purpose," including "the offense type," thereby providing enough information to determine whether a search is legitimate.
"The police cannot police themselves," says Institute for Justice attorney Robert Frommer. His organization argues that a warrant generally should be required to access ALPR data—a policy it aims to establish by challenging ALPR networks on Fourth Amendment grounds and urging states to enact protective legislation.
The congressional response to ALPRs, including several bills and an investigation that Sen. Josh Hawley (R–Mo.) announced last month, has been dominated by conservative Republicans, which confirms that the backlash is not limited to libertarian or left-leaning critics. Whether it will yield effective constraints is another question.
ALPRs are "easily containable," Abbott says, a bit overoptimistically. "They're going to be required to be used responsibly if they're used at all."

articles.title: A Strange Sorting Feature On The Supreme Court's Docket
articles.content:
近日，我注意到美国最高法院案卷系统中存在一个有趣的现象：法官的命令有时会在答辩状记录之前出现，即使答辩状是先提交的。这种情况出现在密苏里州国会选区地图相关案件《霍金斯诉冯·格伦案》中。

答辩状于9月8日清晨提交，而当晚6点左右，巡回法官卡瓦诺在法庭外签署了拒绝申请的命令。然而，在案卷系统中，卡瓦诺的命令却显示在答辩状之前。如果仅从案卷记录看，可能会误以为答辩状是在法官命令之后提交的，这显然不合逻辑。

这个排序方式的原因目前不明确。可能是法官的命令在当天享有优先级别？无论如何，这种记录顺序确实有些奇怪。
articles.summary:
I've noticed a quirk on the Supreme Court's docket. Often, an order from a Justice will be entered before the notation for reply briefs, even though the reply briefs were filed before the order.

Such is the case with Hoskins v. Von Glahn, which concerned Missouri's congressional maps.

The reply briefs were filed in the early hours of Tuesday, September 8. Then, around 6:00 in the evening, Circuit Justice Kavanaugh denied the order in chambers. Yet, on the docket, Kavanaugh's order appears before the reply briefs.

If you were to just look at this docket, you might think that the reply briefs were filed after the Circuit Justice order, which would make no sense.

I'm not sure why they are sorted like this. Perhaps the Justice's order always takes precedence in a given day?

The post A Strange Sorting Feature On The Supreme Court's Docket appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Will It Matter That ABA Council Repealed The DEI Standard?
articles.content:
ABA Standard 206 should have never been adopted. Law school deans rushed it through the process in the wake of George Floyd's death. There was no evidence this standard was necessary or would actually improve race relations. Now, barely six years later, the ABA Council has repealed the standard during an emergency meeting.

What was the rationale for repealing the standard? The Council chair said nothing about the emptiness of Standard 206. Instead the sole reason offered was survival:

"The council believes that national accreditation of law schools is in the best interests of law students, the legal profession and the public, and we can best serve in this role with continued recognition by state supreme courts and the Department of Education," said Melissa Hart, the council's chair, in a statement. "Repealing Standard 206 was necessary to preserve recognition by a growing number of state courts, as well as the department."

The vote was 10-6, with one abstention (a real profile in courage).

Will this action matter? I doubt it. Law schools will still voluntarily comply with the ABA's former Standard through various DEI initiatives. And I doubt the Education Department will care much that this rule was repealed at the barrel of a gun. Nothing stops the ABA from reimposing the same of substantially similar rule in three years.

If only the ABA had listened while there was still a chance. The end is nearer.

The post Will It Matter That ABA Council Repealed The DEI Standard? appeared first on Reason Magazine.
